title: When Leaders Themselves Are Defensive to Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article turns the lens on leaders who dish out candid feedback to their teams but react defensively when they receive criticism from their own superiors. The author points out the double standard: a leader who can't accept feedback themselves raises real doubt in their own manager's mind about their credibility in coaching others. The recommended technique is to avoid arguing in the moment and instead ask a clarifying question, then request time to reflect before responding further. This buys emotional distance, often dissolves the urge to argue, and lets the leader address remaining disagreements calmly and separately — modeling the openness to feedback they expect from their own team.
points: Leaders who give tough feedback to their teams sometimes react defensively to feedback from above.
This double standard raises doubt in senior leaders' minds about a leader's coaching credibility.
The recommended response is to ask a clarifying question and request time before reacting further.
Postponing a reaction lets emotions settle and often reveals the criticism was less objectionable than it felt.
Modeling openness to feedback is framed as essential to a leader's credibility at every level.
quotes: Team members depend on leaders to give them the candid feedback they need to improve their performance.
It’s somewhat surprising how often leaders react defensively when they hear criticisms from their own leader.
Leaders who themselves can’t accept feedback cause grave concern about their ability to lead others.
By postponing the desire to react defensively, a leader buys themselves some time for their emotions to settle and for a more rational view of the criticism they received.
At every level, leaders implicitly know that defensiveness to feedback is not a reaction to what is true or false, but the porous shield of a fragile ego.
When leaders can’t take feedback, they expose themselves as petty and full of false pride.
